questions.topic: Vaccination clinic staffing becomes routine filling mid-shift
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy schedules one pharmacist with six appropriately licensed support workers exclusively for a vaccination clinic under the Board's 2026-02 temporary expanded supervision ratio. During the clinic, the manager directs tw
questions.legal_decision: Stop expanded-ratio routine filling until staff assignments match ordinary permitted ratio.
questions.critical_exception: The 1:6 ratio is limited to qualifying vaccination services, not mixed routine prescription-filling duties.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only a compliant 1:4 or 1:3 support roster actually fills prescriptions, the ordinary filling ratio can be met.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy schedules one pharmacist with six appropriately licensed support workers exclusively for a vaccination clinic under the Board's 2026-02 temporary expanded supervision ratio. During the clinic, the manager directs two of the workers to begin routine outpatient prescription filling, leaving the same six-person staffing arrangement in place. No second pharmacist or staffing waiver is available. What should the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Keep the six-to-one ratio because a vaccination service remains open somewhere in the building.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 2026-02 expanded 1:6 ratio is conditioned on the vaccination-service workflow; it does not authorize ordinary prescription filling by the expanded six-person team.

choices.text: Allow the technicians to fill but suspend all counseling until the clinic closes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Withholding counseling does not cure a staffing ratio violation.

choices.text: Reassign work or add pharmacist coverage so the support workers filling prescriptions comply with the ordinary applicable supervisory ratio.
choices.why: Correct. Under Policy 2026-02 §I, ordinary filling activities require the 1:3 or 1:4 ratio conditions instead of relying on the 1:6 vaccination exception.

choices.text: Require all six support workers to obtain CPR training; this alone converts routine filling into vaccination staffing.
choices.why: Incorrect. CPR credentials do not determine which supervisory ratio applies to routine prescription filling.

choices.text: Have the pharmacist supervise remotely from home while the six workers complete all prescription processing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Nothing in the expanded clinic ratio removes the on-premises pharmacist supervision requirement for routine filling.

questions.topic: Intern consultation requires active preceptor presence despite same-building location
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern begins counseling a patient on a potentially high-risk drug change. The licensed supervising pharmacist is physically elsewhere in the pharmacy reviewing invoices, cannot contemporaneously observe or hear the
questions.legal_decision: Provide active pharmacist direction throughout high-risk counseling.
questions.critical_exception: Being in the same building is not necessarily active consultation supervision.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist were actively available and observing or directing the consultation, the identified supervision failure would be removed.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern begins counseling a patient on a potentially high-risk drug change. The licensed supervising pharmacist is physically elsewhere in the pharmacy reviewing invoices, cannot contemporaneously observe or hear the consultation, and is not monitoring it virtually. A second licensed pharmacist is on-site and available. Which actions are appropriate under Board Policy 2026-02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Allow the intern to complete the consultation independently because the assigned preceptor is somewhere in the building.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section II(C) requires a preceptor actively present in person or virtually for patient or practitioner consultation with material patient-safety implications.

choices.text: Arrange active in-person or virtual pharmacist supervision of the consultation before it proceeds.
choices.why: Correct. Contemporaneous direction or observation by a qualified supervising pharmacist is required for this patient-facing high-risk counseling.

choices.text: Treat the intern's license alone as authority for unsupervised pharmacist-level consultation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Intern licensure does not eliminate direct supervision requirements.

choices.text: Have the available second pharmacist assume and actively provide appropriate direct supervision if the original preceptor cannot.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §II expressly permits a different on-site pharmacist to provide direct supervision when the original preceptor is unavailable.

choices.text: Record counseling as completed by a fully licensed independent pharmacist without changing the actual supervisory arrangements.
choices.why: Incorrect. Documentation does not substitute for required active supervision and must not misrepresent the personnel performing the service.

questions.topic: Sole retail pharmacist wants to leave premises during a permitted break
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has only one pharmacist on duty. After six hours of duty, the pharmacist plans to take a 25-minute meal break and DRIVE to a restaurant two blocks away. Certified technicians would keep the pharmacy open and
questions.legal_decision: Decline sole-pharmacist off-premises break while pharmacy remains open; telephone access cannot replace on-premises presence.
questions.critical_exception: One pharmacist on duty; the break is off-premises while the prescription service remains open.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the sole pharmacist stayed on pharmacy premises during a qualifying break, and all §9.19(17) safeguards were satisfied, the break could be lawful.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has only one pharmacist on duty. After six hours of duty, the pharmacist plans to take a 25-minute meal break and DRIVE to a restaurant two blocks away. Certified technicians would keep the pharmacy open and hand out prescriptions the pharmacist already verified using a compliant log. The pharmacy has written break procedures and the pharmacist can be contacted by telephone. Is the proposed break permissible?

choices.text: No. Without a second on-site pharmacist, the sole on-duty pharmacist cannot leave the premises while the pharmacy remains open.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.19(16)(a),(17)(a) permits an uninterrupted break only while the sole pharmacist remains on the pharmacy premises; telephone contact is not a substitute.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the pharmacist calls every 10 minutes, a certified technician signs the transaction log, and the drug storage area stays secured until the pharmacist returns.
choices.why: Incorrect. A technician log and remote telephone availability do not waive the on-premises requirement.

choices.text: Yes, because previously checked prescriptions are not legally dispensed until the patient pays, so no pharmacist need be present during any part of the meal break.
choices.why: Incorrect. Previously checked prescriptions may be handed off under the limited break procedure only when the sole pharmacist remains on the premises.

choices.text: Yes, provided the store does not fill any new prescriptions during the pharmacist's absence and the patient agrees to receive counseling after the meal break concludes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Suspending new fills does not change the physical on-premises requirement for the sole pharmacist while the pharmacy stays open.

choices.text: No break is ever permitted for a retail pharmacist working more than six consecutive hours, even if the pharmacist remains on premises and follows every Board break condition.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.19(17) expressly permits a qualifying 30-minute break with safeguards while the sole pharmacist remains on premises.

questions.topic: Schedule II perpetual inventory: technician data entry versus discrepancy adjustment
questions.trigger: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a licensed certified pharmacy technician receives an invoiced Schedule II shipment and can correctly enter the documented receipt into the perpetual inventory. A later mandatory physical count shows an unexplain
questions.legal_decision: Separate permitted CII entry from discrepancy investigation and inventory adjustment authorization.
questions.critical_exception: An unexplained discrepancy is not automatically a confirmed reportable theft; investigation is required.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the MOR had completed investigation and made the supported adjustment personally, the specific unauthorized-adjustment defect would not exist.
questions.stem: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a licensed certified pharmacy technician receives an invoiced Schedule II shipment and can correctly enter the documented receipt into the perpetual inventory. A later mandatory physical count shows an unexplained shortage. The Manager of Record (MOR) has not investigated; a technician proposes changing the perpetual balance to match the shelf count and closing the discrepancy. Which steps comply with 247 CMR 9.21(8)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The certified technician may make permitted entries documenting legitimate Schedule II transactions, subject to required controls.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(f) permits a certified pharmacy technician to make entries into the perpetual inventory.

choices.text: The technician may independently write off the unexplained shortage as shrinkage to reconcile the system.
choices.why: Incorrect. Inventory adjustments stemming from a discrepancy are limited to the MOR or, when absent, an authorized pharmacist designee who reports to the MOR.

choices.text: The MOR must investigate the discrepancy and determine any significant-loss or suspected-theft reporting obligations.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(c) assigns discrepancy investigation and applicable reporting to the MOR.

choices.text: A cashier may correct the count if the technician countersigns after closing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(8)(e) prohibits unlicensed personnel from making any entry or adjustment.

choices.text: An adjustment for the discrepancy must be made only by the MOR or the permitted pharmacist designee in the MOR's absence.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specific adjustment rule in 9.21(8)(d).

questions.citation: 247 CMR 9.21(8)(a)–(f); Board Policy 2026-01 where a loss is confirmed

questions.topic: Board investigation demands signed technician delegation records kept by MOR
questions.trigger: During an unannounced Massachusetts pharmacy inspection, a Board investigator requests a current roster of all licensed technician categories, written descriptions of delegated technician duties, and each category's scope of responsibility.
questions.legal_decision: Supply mandated workforce delegation records on request.
questions.critical_exception: Staff badges alone do not describe delegated roles or provide the required roster.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy maintained and produced the specified current written documents, the requested documentation condition would be satisfied.
questions.stem: During an unannounced Massachusetts pharmacy inspection, a Board investigator requests a current roster of all licensed technician categories, written descriptions of delegated technician duties, and each category's scope of responsibility. The MOR has no such documents and says staff badges alone should satisfy the request. Which response is required?

choices.text: Provide badges only; a roster and delegation descriptions are optional when the staff already passed a national exam.
choices.why: Incorrect. National examination status does not replace the documentation duties in 247 CMR 8.06(1).

choices.text: Ask the investigator to return after the next annual pharmacy license renewal before providing employment information.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires these records to be available to the Board upon request.

choices.text: Have the unlicensed store cashier author an oral inventory of staff responsibilities with no written record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 8.06(1) expressly requires a written description of delegated duties and scopes of responsibility.

choices.text: Prepare and provide the current personnel list and written delegated-duty/scope descriptions required of the MOR.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.06(1)(a)–(c) requires these documents to be made available to the Board upon request.

choices.text: Tell the Board that only controlled-substance perpetual inventory records are relevant to an inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. Board inspection authority includes required personnel-related practice records.

questions.topic: On-duty pharmacist detects unsafe sanitation while MOR is offsite
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy's Manager of Record (MOR) is offsite for an approved meeting. The on-duty pharmacist discovers rodent droppings next to a dispensing work surface and a broken sink that prevents appropriate sanitation. The shift sup
questions.legal_decision: On-duty pharmacist reports pharmacy sanitation/repair problems to MOR rather than defer until next inspection.
questions.critical_exception: MOR is away but an on-duty pharmacist independently identifies unsafe physical conditions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the sink and surrounding work area were sanitary and fully functional, no identified repair/sanitation defect would need escalation.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's Manager of Record (MOR) is offsite for an approved meeting. The on-duty pharmacist discovers rodent droppings next to a dispensing work surface and a broken sink that prevents appropriate sanitation. The shift supervisor says the pharmacist should finish the shift without telling the MOR because the MOR will see the condition at the next scheduled inspection. What action is required from the on-duty pharmacist?

choices.text: Wait until the next annual Board inspection because sanitation problems are reportable only after an inspector cites the pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.19(16)(b)3 imposes a direct duty on the on-duty pharmacist to report problems with sanitary conditions or repair to the MOR.

choices.text: Immediately report the identified sanitary and repair problems to the MOR and address product-safety risks before further affected dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(16)(b)3 specifically assigns the report to the on-duty pharmacist, and the pharmacy must avoid compromising safe medication handling.

choices.text: Ask an unlicensed cashier to sign the MOR's name on an inspection report and keep the event confidential from the actual manager.
choices.why: Incorrect. Unauthorized signatures and withholding the defect from the MOR do not meet professional duties.

choices.text: Continue dispensing from the affected work surface but move rodent droppings out of camera view, because product defects require independent laboratory confirmation before any action.
choices.why: Incorrect. An obvious sanitation failure requires professional assessment and reporting; a laboratory finding is not a prerequisite for alerting the MOR.

choices.text: Record the event as a controlled-substance theft even though the pharmacy discovered no theft, diversion or unexplained inventory loss.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated event is a sanitation and repair problem, not a confirmed controlled-substance theft.

questions.topic: Two on-duty pharmacists propose simultaneous meal breaks
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy has two pharmacists scheduled on duty and plans to remain open throughout lunch. Both pharmacists arrange to take their allowed 30-minute breaks AT THE SAME TIME while two certified technicians stay inside
questions.legal_decision: Stagger meal breaks for two-or-more pharmacists rather than invoke lone-pharmacist exception simultaneously.
questions.critical_exception: Two pharmacists are on duty, so staggered-break clause applies despite both remaining physically on premises.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only one pharmacist were on duty and remained on premises during a compliant break, the lone-pharmacist rules would apply rather than the multiple-pharmacist stagger clause.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy has two pharmacists scheduled on duty and plans to remain open throughout lunch. Both pharmacists arrange to take their allowed 30-minute breaks AT THE SAME TIME while two certified technicians stay inside the secured prescription area. The pharmacists say they will remain somewhere on the premises and can both be paged. The pharmacy has otherwise adequate written break procedures. What must the MOR change?

choices.text: Allow the simultaneous breaks because the policy for a lone pharmacist automatically extends to any number of pharmacists on duty.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.19(17)(d) specifically requires staggered breaks when two or more pharmacists are on duty.

choices.text: Have the technicians complete all new clinical and final dispensing validation during the overlap, then ask the pharmacists to sign after returning.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technicians do not acquire independent pharmacist authority during simultaneous breaks.

choices.text: Keep both pharmacists on break together as long as the register labels every handoff a previously validated transaction and stores transaction logs.
choices.why: Incorrect. Recording handoffs does not waive the specific staggered-break requirement for multiple on-duty pharmacists.

choices.text: Require both pharmacists to cancel all meal breaks, because Massachusetts categorically prohibits breaks whenever the pharmacy serves patients.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacist breaks are expressly allowed if the statutory operational safeguards, including staggered timing, are followed.

choices.text: Stagger the pharmacists' meal breaks so they do not both leave active professional duty at once while the pharmacy operates.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.19(17)(d) requires breaks to be staggered when the pharmacy has two or more pharmacists on duty.

questions.topic: Sterile pass-through environmental sample uses cleaner adjacent ISO classification
questions.actor: sterile quality pharmacist; environmental monitoring manager
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy samples a pass-through transfer opening connecting an ISO Class 5 work zone to an ISO Class 7 classified space. Its environmental monitoring worksheet lists a valid surface sample of FOUR CFU per
questions.legal_decision: Apply cleaner ISO side's surface action level to pass-through between different classifications.
questions.critical_exception: Pass-through links ISO5 and ISO7; 4 CFU exceeds ISO5 surface action level.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the interface instead joined ISO7 and ISO8 spaces, the cleaner-side ISO7 threshold, rather than ISO5, would govern.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy samples a pass-through transfer opening connecting an ISO Class 5 work zone to an ISO Class 7 classified space. Its environmental monitoring worksheet lists a valid surface sample of FOUR CFU per contact plate. The manager applies the less stringent ISO Class 7 surface threshold and declares there was no action-level finding. The sample is representative and no other sources of contamination are known. How must this specific sample be assessed?

choices.text: Use the ISO Class 7 limit because the transfer opening is physically closer to the room than to the hood.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2026-03 §I specifically requires the classification of the cleaner space at a pass-through with two different ISO classifications.

choices.text: Ignore the sample entirely because pass-through locations do not appear in the environmental monitoring program.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy expressly provides for pass-through action levels and does not exclude their samples.

choices.text: Apply the ISO Class 5 surface action level because the cleaner adjacent space determines the threshold; 4 CFU exceeds the ISO 5 action limit.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §I directs pass-throughs to use the cleaner space's ISO classification, and the ISO 5 surface action threshold is exceeded at 4 CFU.

choices.text: Automatically treat 4 CFU as a federal controlled-substance loss and file DEA Form 106.
choices.why: Incorrect. A surface bioburden finding is an environmental quality issue, not inventory theft or significant loss.

choices.text: Average the two ISO surface action levels and round them upward without documenting the actual organisms or sample site.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's pass-through instruction is to use the cleaner ISO classification, not a mathematical mean of two limits.

questions.citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-03 §I (Surface Environmental Monitoring action-level table and pass-through footnote)

questions.topic: ISO Class 8 remediation BUD differs by sterile versus nonsterile starting components
questions.trigger: During remediation of an action-level VIABLE environmental result in an ISO Class 8 area, a Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy has completed the required initial assessment, risk assessment and approved remediation plan. The Board h
questions.legal_decision: Choose distinct ISO8 viable-remediation refrigerated CSP BUD according to sterile/nonsterile starting components.
questions.critical_exception: ISO Class 8/ISO7 nonbuffer, viable action-level remediation permitted; sterile versus nonsterile starting materials cause 10d versus 4d maximum.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Replacing all nonsterile starting components of batch N with sterile starting components changes the temporary refrigerated BUD ceiling from 4 days to 10 days if all other requirements remain satisfied.
questions.stem: During remediation of an action-level VIABLE environmental result in an ISO Class 8 area, a Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy has completed the required initial assessment, risk assessment and approved remediation plan. The Board has not imposed additional restrictions, and continued compounding in that area is otherwise permitted under Board Policy 2026-03. Two prospective CSP batches differ only in that batch S is prepared exclusively from STERILE starting components and batch N uses at least one NONSTERILE starting component. What maximum refrigerated BUDs does the state policy allow during the remediation?

choices.text: Four days for both batches, because all ISO Class 8 remediation CSPs are treated as if they use nonsterile starting materials.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2026-03 §V distinguishes BUDs for sterile-only versus nonsterile starting components in ISO7 nonbuffer and ISO8 areas.

choices.text: Thirty days for batch S and ten days for batch N, because sterile starting materials waive the temporary remediation limits.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither starting material category has such a 30-day default exemption during the affected-area viable remediation.

choices.text: Ten days for both batches, provided the operator documents a successful process simulation before production.
choices.why: Incorrect. Process simulation does not override the specified shorter temporary BUD for batches with nonsterile starting components.

choices.text: Up to ten days refrigerated for batch S, and up to four days refrigerated for batch N, subject to every other applicable restriction.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §V for ISO7 nonbuffer and ISO8 rooms assigns 10 days refrigerated for sterile starting components and 4 days refrigerated if any nonsterile component is used.

choices.text: No refrigerated BUD may ever be assigned to a CSP made during any viable EM remediation, even if the Board's risk-based temporary pathway explicitly permits compounding.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section V contains a conditional temporary compounding pathway with specified BUD limits for the affected ISO classes.

questions.citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-03 §V (ISO Class 7 except buffer rooms, ISO Class 8 areas: starting component-specific BUD)

questions.topic: Only affected ISO Class 5 hood: temporary immediate-use CSP exception
questions.trigger: An institutional sterile-compounding pharmacy has only ONE ISO Class 5 PEC. Viable environmental monitoring identifies an action-level finding directly in that PEC. The pharmacy begins an appropriate documented response and product-risk ass
questions.legal_decision: Allow at most absolutely necessary USP-qualified immediate-use compounding in sole affected ISO5 PEC until remediation, not ordinary sterile production.
questions.critical_exception: Single affected ISO5 PEC, not multiple unaffected PECs; immediate-use threshold and otherwise safe remediation circumstances assumed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: With a separate unaffected certified ISO5 PEC and a supportive risk assessment, §V(B) could permit compounding in that unaffected PEC without invoking the sole-PEC immediate-use exception.
questions.stem: An institutional sterile-compounding pharmacy has only ONE ISO Class 5 PEC. Viable environmental monitoring identifies an action-level finding directly in that PEC. The pharmacy begins an appropriate documented response and product-risk assessment, but remediation has not yet been completed. A prescriber requests urgent access to a CSP that satisfies all USP <797> IMMEDIATE-USE conditions; the pharmacy has no unaffected ISO Class 5 PEC, and the Board has not ordered a broader restriction. Which action is supportable under Board Policy 2026-03?

choices.text: Resume routine Category 2 production in the affected hood because a physician considers the CSP clinically urgent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2026-03 §V generally prohibits normal compounding in an affected ISO5 PEC until proper remediation.

choices.text: Use the contaminated hood for ordinary stockpiling if a certified technician documents a deep cleaning without verifying remediation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Routine stock compounding is not authorized simply because cleaning was attempted.

choices.text: Treat any sterile CSP as immediate-use after removing its printed BUD label, without checking USP immediate-use criteria.
choices.why: Incorrect. The immediate-use pathway depends on the actual USP-defined requirements, not a label modification.

choices.text: Wait until the next annual license inspection to decide whether the action-level result needs remediation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Environmental action-level findings require prompt reporting, assessment and remediation under Board policy.

choices.text: Only if absolutely necessary, consider an immediate-use CSP under its actual USP criteria; do not restart ordinary affected-PEC compounding before remediation.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §V(C) permits only USP-defined immediate-use CSPs if absolutely necessary when a pharmacy has a sole affected ISO5 PEC, subject to all other safety conditions.

questions.citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-03 §V (ISO Class 5 Area(s), particularly subsection C); USP <797> immediate-use provisions

questions.topic: Nonviable particle action level: cannot use viable BUD exception to keep compounding
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts compounding pharmacy's ISO Class 7 secondary engineering control fails the action-level NONVIABLE particle count. Staff immediately establish a remediation plan, but the affected classified rooms have not been fully remediat
questions.legal_decision: Suspend affected sterile compounding on nonviable action result until remediated and recertified.
questions.critical_exception: §V temporary viable BUDs do not substitute for nonviable-action full remediation and recertification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the result instead were a viable action level and §V requirements were met, limited compounding with temporary BUDs could be considered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts compounding pharmacy's ISO Class 7 secondary engineering control fails the action-level NONVIABLE particle count. Staff immediately establish a remediation plan, but the affected classified rooms have not been fully remediated or recertified. A supervisor argues that the pharmacy can continue compounding with the temporary 24-hour BUD used for some VIABLE microbial excursions. What is the correct distinction?

choices.text: Continue any Category 2 production as long as the ISO Class 5 hood has passed its last gloved fingertip test.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy imposes an affected-area suspension and recertification requirement for nonviable particle action levels.

choices.text: Reclassify the excursion as viable because viable-results rules permit temporary BUDs.
choices.why: Incorrect. The type of environmental failure must be interpreted accurately; the viable pathway does not override §III(D).

choices.text: Use only a shortened BUD and skip any recertification if the product is urgently needed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy explicitly requires full remediation and recertification for action-level nonviable particle counts unless the Board directs otherwise.

choices.text: Suspend compounding in the affected operation until full remediation and recertification of classified areas, unless the Board directs otherwise.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §III(D) treats nonviable particulate action levels differently from the limited viable remediation pathway.

choices.text: Change the sample date in the record and treat the result as no longer actionable.
choices.why: Incorrect. Falsifying records does not satisfy environmental monitoring and reporting requirements.

questions.topic: Defective simple nonsterile compound dispensed: recall without automatic seven-day Board defective-report trigger
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispensed a patient-specific SIMPLE nonsterile compounded cream. Later laboratory testing establishes a harmful potency defect; patients have not reported a serious adverse event, and the preparation is no
questions.legal_decision: Recall defective simple CNSP and log; distinguish specific Board defect report scope.
questions.critical_exception: Dispensed simple CNSP, no suspected serious adverse drug event, not complex category.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the compounded product were sterile or classified as complex CNSP, Policy 2024-04's seven-day Board defective-preparation notification would apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispensed a patient-specific SIMPLE nonsterile compounded cream. Later laboratory testing establishes a harmful potency defect; patients have not reported a serious adverse event, and the preparation is not classified as complex nonsterile. The pharmacy immediately identifies another patient who received the same preparation. Does Board Policy 2024-04 permit waiting for an adverse event before acting, and does its seven-day defective-preparation report automatically apply?

choices.text: Wait until a patient develops serious injury because a simple nonsterile preparation is excluded from all recall rules.
choices.why: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.112 §39D(e) and Policy 2024-04 require immediate recall whenever a compounded preparation may be defective.

choices.text: Keep distributing the stock and submit only a normal CQI report, because the pharmacy is not a sterile compounder.
choices.why: Incorrect. Compounded defective products already dispensed trigger recall obligations regardless of sterility category.

choices.text: Report every simple nonsterile defect to DEA Form 106 within one business day and dispense unaffected-looking units.
choices.why: Incorrect. DEA Form 106 concerns theft/significant loss, and a simple CNSP defect is not automatically reportable under this policy's seven-day Board defect rule.

choices.text: Keep the remaining compounded stock available but email recipients when a complaint arrives.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy requires segregation, no further dispensing, and immediate recipient contact upon recall.

choices.text: Immediately recall and quarantine the defect, contact recipients and maintain the defective-drug log; the policy's seven-day defect report is specific to CSPs or complex CNSPs.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2024-04 and §39D(e) require immediate recall and appropriate records for any defective dispensed compound, whereas its specific seven-day Board report covers defective CSPs and complex-category CNSPs.

questions.topic: Defective compounded preparation discovered before dispensing
questions.trigger: A pharmacy's pharmacist identifies an out-of-specification compounded nonsterile batch during an internal quality check before any part has been dispensed or distributed. The batch remains secured within the pharmacy. There is no patient ex
questions.legal_decision: Hold undistributed defective compound; CQI documentation recommended; no automatic defective-CSP Board report.
questions.critical_exception: No compounded product dispensed; no SADE; no other report triggers.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an affected preparation had already been dispensed, the immediate recall/recipient notification and applicable Board defective-preparation report obligations would change.
questions.stem: A pharmacy's pharmacist identifies an out-of-specification compounded nonsterile batch during an internal quality check before any part has been dispensed or distributed. The batch remains secured within the pharmacy. There is no patient exposure or suspected serious adverse drug event. Which actions are supported by Board Policy 2024-04? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Prevent dispensing of the out-of-specification preparation and correct or dispose of it lawfully as appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Product integrity requires withholding defective material from patient distribution.

choices.text: Contact all patients to announce a product recall even though no patient has received any batch unit.
choices.why: Incorrect. The mandatory recipient recall/contact pathway presupposes dispensed or distributed affected drug preparations.

choices.text: Automatically submit the seven-day Board defective-drug notification because the batch was compounded, regardless of distribution status.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2024-04 specifically says defects discovered before dispensing do not need to be reported through that Board form.

choices.text: Continue dispensing if the product's original calculated BUD has not passed.
choices.why: Incorrect. A computed BUD does not override confirmed potency or quality failure.

choices.text: Document this pre-dispensing event in the pharmacy's CQI process as recommended; the Board's specific defective-preparation form is not mandatory for that undistributed batch.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2024-04 specifically recommends CQI documentation for defects found before dispensing and says these events do not need Board defective-drug reporting.

questions.topic: DSCSA illegitimate drug confirmation: 24-hour notification after investigation
questions.trigger: A pharmacy has quarantined a suspicious prescription-drug shipment and investigated it with the manufacturer. The manufacturer verifies that several packages are counterfeit; the pharmacy has determined the product is illegitimate. Records
questions.legal_decision: Confirm illegitimate product, notify FDA/trading partners within 24h, prevent dispensing and disposition.
questions.critical_exception: Counterfeit verified; this is beyond merely a suspect product awaiting investigation.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If investigation reliably cleared the shipment as legitimate, §582(d)(4)(B)'s confirmed-illegitimate notification rule would not be triggered.
questions.stem: A pharmacy has quarantined a suspicious prescription-drug shipment and investigated it with the manufacturer. The manufacturer verifies that several packages are counterfeit; the pharmacy has determined the product is illegitimate. Records show some units were already transferred to an immediate trading partner, and unshipped units remain quarantined. The team proposes waiting for a wholesaler's monthly meeting before reporting. Under FD&C Act §582(d)(4), which steps are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Notify FDA and immediate trading partners believed to have received the illegitimate product within 24 hours of that determination.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(B)(ii) requires notification to FDA and immediate partners likely to have received the product not later than 24 hours after the illegitimacy determination.

choices.text: Disposition the illegitimate products under pharmacy control and assist affected trading partners with disposition as required.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(B)(i) imposes these controls and cooperation duties.

choices.text: Release the quarantine because the manufacturer confirmed the product's identity as counterfeit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Confirmation of illegitimacy demands disposition, not release into patient dispensing stock.

choices.text: Keep required investigation and disposition records for the applicable federal retention period.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(A)(iv) requires suspect investigation records for at least six years after conclusion; associated illegitimate-product records remain subject to applicable record requirements.

choices.text: Notify FDA only when a patient reports an injury; confirmed counterfeit stock by itself requires no notification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statutory notification trigger is the determination of illegitimacy, not a patient harm report.

questions.topic: DSCSA product delivered without required trace records: obtain documentation before acceptance
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a new bulk shipment of covered prescription drugs from its usual licensed wholesale distributor. Shipping boxes are intact, but the distributor has provided no required DSCSA product tracing informat
questions.legal_decision: Resolve missing required transaction documentation before treating shipment as eligible saleable inventory.
questions.critical_exception: No special federal small-dispenser tracing exemption applies to this transaction and no evidence of counterfeiting established.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a valid transaction-specific exemption removed the particular tracing obligation and authenticity checks were satisfied, document receipt under that exemption instead.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a new bulk shipment of covered prescription drugs from its usual licensed wholesale distributor. Shipping boxes are intact, but the distributor has provided no required DSCSA product tracing information, and no applicable transaction exemption applies. Management says the pharmacy can permanently accept the product into saleable stock because the seller is trusted and supply is short. What is the best first compliance action?

choices.text: Accept the shipment without tracing documents because the supplier has a current distributor license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Trading-partner authorization and product-tracing documentation are separate obligations under §582(d)(1).

choices.text: Add an invented trace record showing a typical manufacturer and release all units.
choices.why: Incorrect. Fabricated records cannot substitute for required tracing information and undermine supply-chain integrity.

choices.text: Obtain the required tracing information from the trading partner and hold release until its receipt and legitimacy are appropriately established.
choices.why: Correct. FD&C Act §582(d)(1)(A) requires required transaction documentation with ownership transfer, and FDA advises dispensers to work with trading partners to obtain missing documents.

choices.text: Treat every missing invoice automatically as proof of an illegitimate counterfeit requiring a 24-hour notice.
choices.why: Incorrect. Missing transaction documentation must be resolved; it does not by itself prove the separate 'illegitimate product' notification threshold.

choices.text: Ignore the missing records for six years because trace documentation is required only after a pharmacy resells the medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Dispenser tracing obligations apply when accepting ownership, and records generally must be maintained for six years.

questions.citation: 21 U.S.C. §360eee-1(d)(1)(A)(i)–(iii); FDA 'Pharmacists: Utilize DSCSA Requirements to Protect Your Patients'

questions.topic: Patient refuses after-hours automated pickup: right to non-APS option
questions.trigger: A pharmacy has an appropriately secured, approved Automated Pharmacy System (APS) in the same building. The prescription is for an ordinary Schedule VI medicine eligible for APS release, and pharmacist consultation is available by phone. A
questions.legal_decision: Respect patient choice not to use an otherwise lawful APS.
questions.critical_exception: The eligible APS cannot be forced on a patient as the exclusive option.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the patient freely chose APS and all other conditions were met, APS use could be lawful.
questions.stem: A pharmacy has an appropriately secured, approved Automated Pharmacy System (APS) in the same building. The prescription is for an ordinary Schedule VI medicine eligible for APS release, and pharmacist consultation is available by phone. A patient says they do not want to use the machine, asks to receive medication through the normal pharmacy counter when it opens, and is not asking for earlier delivery. What should the pharmacy do?

choices.text: Honor the patient's decision not to use APS and arrange a conventional pharmacy handoff rather than make machine use mandatory.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.10(1)(h) requires allowing the patient to choose whether or not to use the APS; the pharmacy may provide another lawful handoff.

choices.text: Require machine pickup because the prescription was already filled and eligible for APS dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. APS eligibility does not remove the patient's express choice not to use it.

choices.text: Delete the patient's prescription if they decline APS; no nonautomated option may be offered.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule does not require cancellation when APS is declined.

choices.text: Transfer the order into an unlicensed retail pickup machine because the patient refused the licensed APS.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing machines does not create lawful dispensing authorization.

choices.text: Charge the patient an extra controlled-substance transfer fee solely as a condition of refusing APS.
choices.why: Incorrect. An APS choice is not authorization to impose a punitive refusal fee or circumvent transfer rules.

questions.topic: Uncontaminated ISO Class 5 PEC during remediation of another PEC
questions.trigger: A sterile compounding pharmacy has TWO separate certified ISO Class 5 PECs in its classified compounding suite. Environmental monitoring finds an action-level VIABLE result inside PEC A; PEC B and its surrounding classified area show no imp
questions.legal_decision: Continue only genuinely unaffected PECs after documented risk assessment, not implicated PEC.
questions.critical_exception: Two separate PECs; viable ISO5 action in A; B is not implicated; no Board-wide stop.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If both PECs showed action-level contamination or the assessment could not establish unaffected status, continuing in PEC B would not be supported.
questions.stem: A sterile compounding pharmacy has TWO separate certified ISO Class 5 PECs in its classified compounding suite. Environmental monitoring finds an action-level VIABLE result inside PEC A; PEC B and its surrounding classified area show no implicated contamination. The pharmacy has already performed an immediate root-cause assessment, initiated a remediation and product-risk plan, and scheduled repeat sampling. The Board has not directed a complete shutdown. Which statements follow Board Policy 2026-03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Both PECs must always be closed until PEC A is recertified, even when assessment shows PEC B is unaffected.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2026-03 §V expressly permits continued compounding in unaffected ISO 5 PECs when the documented risk assessment deems it appropriate.

choices.text: The pharmacy may continue compounding in PEC B if the risk assessment supports its being unaffected and all other requirements remain met.
choices.why: Correct. Section V, ISO Class 5 Area(s) B, allows the unaffected PEC to continue with suitable risk assessment.

choices.text: The pharmacy may use PEC A for ordinary Category 2 work immediately because PEC B is uncontaminated.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section V(A) restricts resumption in the affected ISO 5 PEC until proper remediation, subject to the specific limited exception.

choices.text: PEC A generally must not resume ordinary compounding before remediation; product risk from the excursion still requires review.
choices.why: Correct. Section V(A) restricts affected-PEC compounding while §§III–IV require appropriate remediation and assessment.

choices.text: Once PEC B stays open, the pharmacy no longer needs to notify the Board or investigate PEC A's action-level result.
choices.why: Incorrect. Permitted operation of an unaffected hood does not waive required reporting and remediation for the affected hood.

questions.citation: Board Policy 2026-03 §§II–V, especially §V ISO Class 5 Area(s) A–B

questions.topic: LTCF discontinuation: controlled-drug collection within three business days
questions.actor: LTCF director of nursing; authorized pharmacy collector
questions.trigger: A resident of a Massachusetts long-term care facility dies on Monday. The facility holds that resident's lawful Schedule II medication previously dispensed to the resident. A DEA-authorized retail-pharmacy collector maintains a properly reg
questions.legal_decision: Dispose discontinued LTCF ultimate-user controlled drug in authorized LTCF collection receptacle within 3 business days.
questions.critical_exception: DEA-modified collector at LTCF, drug dispensed to resident (not pharmacy stock), death Monday; Wednesday stipulated normal business day.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If discontinued use occurred only on Thursday, a Monday disposal in that onsite receptacle could still fall within the prescribed three-business-day window.
questions.stem: A resident of a Massachusetts long-term care facility dies on Monday. The facility holds that resident's lawful Schedule II medication previously dispensed to the resident. A DEA-authorized retail-pharmacy collector maintains a properly registered collection receptacle at the LTCF. On Friday, facility staff plan to dispose of the drug in that receptacle for the first time; Wednesday was a state holiday but was still an ordinary business day for the facility and collector. The facility has not taken another authorized disposal route. What is the applicable federal time limit?

choices.text: The LTCF can keep the medicine indefinitely if it remains inside an individually labeled, locked resident medication drawer.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1317.80(a) sets a prompt disposal deadline when the LTCF uses an authorized LTCF collection receptacle after discontinuation, including death.

choices.text: Transfer the controlled drug to that authorized LTCF receptacle immediately and no later than three business days after discontinuation; the Friday plan exceeds that window under the stipulated business-day facts.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.80(a) sets a three-business-day outer limit for LTCF transfer into its authorized onsite receptacle after death, transfer, or treatment discontinuation.

choices.text: Place the drug in the pharmacy's own expired-inventory reverse distributor bin because all LTCF resident medicines become pharmacy inventory upon death.
choices.why: Incorrect. This is a drug previously lawfully possessed for the ultimate user; the applicable collector mechanism is not automatically the pharmacy's registrant-owned stock process.

choices.text: Wait until 30 days after the resident's death because the DEA collection time limit begins only when the facility conducts monthly controlled counts.
choices.why: Incorrect. The three-business-day timeframe is tied to discontinuation of use, not monthly inventory timing.

choices.text: A facility employee can make the resident's medication part of another resident's medication supply without a new prescription because the original resident is deceased.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescription identity and controlled-substance law prohibit using one patient's patient-specific medicine as another patient's routine stock.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1317.80(a) (discontinuation, death or transfer; 3-business-day LTCF disposal when using authorized receptacle)

questions.topic: Defective DEA Form 222 cannot be corrected at supplier
questions.actor: wholesale supplier and retail pharmacy purchasing pharmacist
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy submits a properly signed paper DEA Form 222 to a distributor to purchase Schedule II stock. After the purchaser executed the form, a distributor employee notices that the item description was altered in ink.
questions.legal_decision: Reject altered DEA Form 222, return original plus reason, retain defect record, replace with new valid form.
questions.critical_exception: Original form displays an actual alteration; the §1305.15 nonacceptance rule applies, not ordinary partial shipment.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the paper order remained complete, unaltered and properly executed, it could be evaluated for filling under the regular §1305.13 rules.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy submits a properly signed paper DEA Form 222 to a distributor to purchase Schedule II stock. After the purchaser executed the form, a distributor employee notices that the item description was altered in ink. The distributor offers to initial the change and fill the form without returning it. The purchaser agrees that the submitted paper order bears an unauthorized alteration. What is the correct workflow?

choices.text: The supplier may complete the order as written because a correction initial always cures post-execution alterations on DEA Form 222.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1305.15(a)(2) expressly prohibits filling a Form 222 that shows an alteration, erasure or change of description.

choices.text: The supplier can ignore the alteration after verifying the pharmacy's DEA registration through its online database.
choices.why: Incorrect. Registration verification and the separate requirement that DEA Form 222 be complete, properly executed and unaltered are cumulative obligations.

choices.text: The supplier must return the original unaccepted Form 222 with an explanation; the purchaser retains it and must execute a new compliant Form 222.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1305.15(b),(d) requires return with a statement, retention of the defective form/statement, and a new valid 222 rather than a correction.

choices.text: A technician can convert the original Schedule II purchase into a Schedule IV invoice if the distributor still wants to provide the same drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. The controlled schedule remains II and cannot be changed by purchase-invoice labeling or staff convenience.

choices.text: A supplier may erase the altered description and then ship a partial quantity within 60 days after the original order's issuance.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 60-day partial-shipment option does not authorize filling a defective or altered Form 222.

questions.topic: Unfilled paper DEA Form 222 lost in transit before distributor receives it
questions.actor: pharmacy registrant purchaser; original CII supplier
questions.trigger: A DEA-registered Massachusetts pharmacy mails a properly executed original DEA Form 222 to its Schedule II supplier. The pharmacy later confirms the order was lost while in transit, no containers were furnished, and the supplier never recei
questions.legal_decision: Issue compliant replacement Form 222 with original form identification and not-received statement; segregate rejected recovered original.
questions.critical_exception: Lost in transit; none of original ordered goods received, unlike theft/loss of blank forms on the pharmacy premises.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the original form had arrived and the supplier had already filled it, the unfilled-in-transit replacement procedure would not justify another equivalent shipment.
questions.stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts pharmacy mails a properly executed original DEA Form 222 to its Schedule II supplier. The pharmacy later confirms the order was lost while in transit, no containers were furnished, and the supplier never received that original. The pharmacist wants to reorder promptly without causing the original order to be filled a second time if recovered. What documentation procedure is correct?

choices.text: Send an email requesting goods under the same lost Form 222 number, and omit all records because no stock arrived.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1305.16(a) specifies a replacement Form 222 and written statement/copy retention procedure for an unfilled lost form.

choices.text: Change the mailing date on the pharmacy's archived photocopy to generate a new controlling original Form 222.
choices.why: Incorrect. Altering an archival copy does not create a valid replacement order.

choices.text: Telephone the supplier to fill the missing original and disregard the risk that the first signed original could later be recovered.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly provides a new form, a statement documenting the original and a supplier response if the first original appears.

choices.text: Execute a new DEA Form 222 with the required lost-form number/date and no-goods-received statement; retain/send the specified copies and instruct the supplier to mark any recovered original 'Not accepted.'
choices.why: Correct. This is the replacement protocol under 21 CFR 1305.16(a), including retention and recovered original disposition.

choices.text: Convert the lost Schedule II paper order into an ordinary verbal Schedule III invoice and let the supplier ship the identical drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. A lost CII ordering form cannot be replaced by a verbal or nonscheduled invoice.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1305.16(a) (unfilled DEA Form 222 lost in transmission)

questions.topic: LTCF collector liner exchange: authorized staffing combinations
questions.actor: pharmacy authorized collector and LTCF charge nurse
questions.trigger: A DEA-authorized retail pharmacy operates a controlled-substance collection receptacle inside a Massachusetts long-term care facility under an appropriately modified DEA registration. The inner liner is full and must be removed and replaced
questions.legal_decision: Use permitted authorized-collector + LTCF supervisor staffing to change authorized onsite LTCF collection liner.
questions.critical_exception: Registered LTCF receptacle, collector employee plus designated supervisor-level LTCF employee.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If neither the collector's designated LTCF supervisor nor a second collector employee were present, the proposed single-collector staff team would be insufficient.
questions.stem: A DEA-authorized retail pharmacy operates a controlled-substance collection receptacle inside a Massachusetts long-term care facility under an appropriately modified DEA registration. The inner liner is full and must be removed and replaced. Exactly one employee of the authorized pharmacy collector is present, along with the LTCF's designated charge nurse who is a supervisor-level LTCF employee. A second collector employee cannot attend. Under 21 CFR 1317.80, which procedures are permissible? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The one collector employee and the designated supervisor-level LTCF employee may perform or supervise the liner removal and installation under the permitted LTCF staffing alternative.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.80(c) allows one authorized collector employee plus one supervisor-level LTCF employee designated by the collector, as an alternative to two collector employees.

choices.text: Any two LTCF residents may install and remove the inner liner without the authorized collector's employee because the liner belongs to the LTCF.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1317.80(c) defines the authorized personnel alternatives and does not permit an unsupervised residents-only handling process.

choices.text: Two employees of the authorized collector would be another expressly permitted staffing arrangement, even without the charge nurse participating.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1317.80(c) separately permits two authorized collector employees.

choices.text: Facility staff may open an already-sealed liner and hand-sort individual tablets so that controlled-substance counts can be corrected.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal collection rules prohibit individually handling, sorting and accounting for deposited medications after collection.

choices.text: A noncollector office courier may independently transport unsealed liners to an off-site locker without required registered collector controls.
choices.why: Incorrect. The collector manages and maintains the receptacle and its liners under the regulated transfer and custody procedures.

questions.topic: Confirmed theft of an ordinary Massachusetts Schedule VI medicine: state report versus DEA Form 106
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy discovers camera evidence that an employee intentionally diverted 12 tablets of an ordinary prescription-only Massachusetts Schedule VI medicine that is NOT federally controlled and is NOT a PMP-desi
questions.legal_decision: Report any confirmed employee diversion of MA Schedule VI to Board, without inventing DEA Form106.
questions.critical_exception: Confirmed theft/pilferage; MA-only SVI, not federally controlled; no PMP reporting status.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If investigation showed only an insignificant unexplained non-theft loss, the policy's Section III onsite documentation/trending pathway could apply instead.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy discovers camera evidence that an employee intentionally diverted 12 tablets of an ordinary prescription-only Massachusetts Schedule VI medicine that is NOT federally controlled and is NOT a PMP-designated Schedule VI drug. The loss has been CONFIRMED. The owner argues that no reporting is needed because the amount is small and the drug is not Schedule II–V. Which conclusions follow from Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-01? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Report the confirmed employee diversion to the Board within seven calendar days using the required pharmacy loss reporting process.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-01 §II(A) covers every theft, employee pilferage or diversion regardless of quantity or schedule.

choices.text: File a federal DEA Form 106 for this Schedule VI-only drug solely because it is controlled under Massachusetts law.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal DEA Form 106 theft/significant loss system applies to federally controlled substances; this ordinary Schedule VI drug is not DEA scheduled.

choices.text: Do not document the event because it involves a medication outside MassPAT reporting.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy's employee pilferage category does not require PMP reporting status to be reportable.

choices.text: Preserve investigation records, report under the applicable Massachusetts confirmed-theft policy, and address any other applicable state/local reporting.
choices.why: Correct. The Board policy imposes a timely RLCS state report and separately requires compliance with other applicable authorities.

choices.text: Classify the diversion as an insignificant nonreportable unexplained loss without considering confirmed employee intent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section III's insignificant-loss documentation-only provision does not excuse theft or employee diversion that is confirmed.

questions.topic: Scheduled medication incompatible with multi-drug single-dose adherence pack
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares a patient's 30-day multidrug single-dose adherence pouches. The daily maintenance regimen contains a Schedule III medication, a Schedule IV medicine and two Schedule VI tablets; all are intended for schedul
questions.legal_decision: Separate Schedule III drug from otherwise lawful daily CIV/VI multi-drug compliance packs.
questions.critical_exception: Schedule III is prohibited even for fixed daily medication and 30-day supply.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the entire daily regimen were only compatible Schedule IV and VI non-PRN medications, the Schedule II/III exclusion would not block this specific packaging.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares a patient's 30-day multidrug single-dose adherence pouches. The daily maintenance regimen contains a Schedule III medication, a Schedule IV medicine and two Schedule VI tablets; all are intended for scheduled daily use, not as needed, and are otherwise compatible with the pouches. The pharmacist proposes putting every drug in each daily combined pouch because 30 days is under the 60-day packaging cap. What must change?

choices.text: Use the 30-day package exactly as proposed because the 60-day maximum overrides all Schedule exclusions in the compliance-packaging rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 60-day maximum is separate from the categorical prohibition on including Schedule II or III in a multi-drug-single-dose package.

choices.text: Exclude only Schedule VI drugs, because Massachusetts permits combined packaging for all federally controlled medications.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(3)(b) specifically excludes Schedule II and III—not IV and VI—from these multi-drug packages.

choices.text: Move the Schedule III drug into a different, lawful patient-specific package; use eligible daily Schedule IV/VI medicines in compliant multi-drug pouches.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(3)(b) prohibits Schedule III in multi-drug-single-dose packaging but allows compatible scheduled Schedule IV/VI products if other requirements are met.

choices.text: Change the patient directions to 'PRN' so that Schedule III drugs are permitted in multi-drug packs.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(3)(c) separately prohibits as-needed medicines; falsifying directions would add another violation.

choices.text: Remove the patient's name from all pouches and treat the schedule conflict as resolved through anonymized packaging.
choices.why: Incorrect. A labeling change does not eliminate the Schedule II/III prohibition in 9.08(3)(b).

questions.topic: Dispensing restricted-control prescription without physical ID under documented severe hardship
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives an authentic Schedule II prescription and confirms the legitimate medical purpose. The patient's authorized agent comes to pick it up after a sudden house fire destroyed the agent's wallet and all governm
questions.legal_decision: Apply serious-hardship statutory exception using pharmacist documentation and agent printed/signed name and address.
questions.critical_exception: Agent lacks government identification due disaster, serious hardship documented; no other controlled-drug validity problem.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the agent merely refused identification for convenience and the pharmacist could not establish serious hardship, the exception could not be invoked.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives an authentic Schedule II prescription and confirms the legitimate medical purpose. The patient's authorized agent comes to pick it up after a sudden house fire destroyed the agent's wallet and all government ID. The agent can print a name and address in the pharmacy log and sign it. Based on reliable case details, the pharmacist reasonably believes that withholding the medicine today would cause serious hardship to the patient and documents the basis. May the pharmacist use the narrow pickup-ID exception?

choices.text: No. Massachusetts law imposes an unconditional in-person photo-ID requirement with no hardship exception for any Schedule II–V dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.04(14)(c) expressly recognizes an exception for serious hardship and requires written identity/log attestations.

choices.text: Yes, but only after changing the Schedule II drug into Schedule VI in the pharmacy's computerized record.
choices.why: Incorrect. State Schedule classification cannot be altered to avoid positive identification rules.

choices.text: Yes, simply by accepting the agent's verbal name; no documentation of hardship or signature is required.
choices.why: Incorrect. The hardship rationale and printed name/address with signature must be documented under 9.04(14)(c).

choices.text: No, because the customer's agent may never pick up a patient's Schedule II medicine in Massachusetts.
choices.why: Incorrect. Sections 9.04(14)(a)–(c) expressly account for ultimate users or their agents.

choices.text: Yes, the pharmacist may use the documented serious-hardship exception if the agent prints name/address and signs the required log, with all other rules met.
choices.why: Correct. The explicit §9.04(14)(c) criteria are satisfied by the described serious-hardship finding, pharmacist documentation and agent's printed/signed identity record.

questions.topic: Rejected Board inspection plan of correction: seven-day resubmission deadline
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy submits its initial inspection plan of correction within the prescribed deadline. The Board rejects it as inadequate because several cited violations have no responsible person or implementation date. The MOR states
questions.legal_decision: Submit revised POC within seven days after rejection; include action, owner and dates.
questions.critical_exception: Returned unacceptable initial plan, not merely the original report issuance.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An initial inspection report with no previously submitted POC triggers the initial 21-day or Board-directed timeframe, not this seven-day revision clock.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy submits its initial inspection plan of correction within the prescribed deadline. The Board rejects it as inadequate because several cited violations have no responsible person or implementation date. The MOR states that the pharmacy gets another 21 days automatically for revisions. Which action follows 247 CMR 9.25(5)?

choices.text: The pharmacy need not revise its plan because the original plan was submitted within its initial deadline.
choices.why: Incorrect. An unacceptable plan returned by the Board must be revised; timeliness of the first submission does not cure its omissions.

choices.text: Submit an acceptable revised plan within seven days after the Board returns the deficient plan.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.25(5) specifies a seven-day revised-plan deadline after return of an unacceptable plan.

choices.text: Wait for the next annual self-inspection and present the corrections only then.
choices.why: Incorrect. The mandatory revised-plan deadline is independent of annual self-inspection.

choices.text: Replace every cited violation with a general statement of intent and omit completion dates.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.25(2) requires corrective action, expected implementation date, and responsible person(s).

choices.text: Have a billing contractor sign the revised plan instead of the MOR because pharmacy technicians caused the original deficiencies.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.25(3) requires the MOR and applicable supervising licensee signatures.

questions.topic: Medication refrigerator excursion: integrity, logging, food ban and retention
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy keeps vaccines and refrigerated prescription drugs in a household dorm-style refrigerator with a freezer compartment opening directly into the refrigerated space. A logged overnight temperature excursion o
questions.legal_decision: Use approved fridge, document/assess excursion, retain logs one year, and no food.
questions.critical_exception: No product-specific temperature stability determination yet exists; do not automatically release stock.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a compliant refrigerator had maintained temperatures within range and no integrity concern existed, the excursion-response hold would not be triggered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy keeps vaccines and refrigerated prescription drugs in a household dorm-style refrigerator with a freezer compartment opening directly into the refrigerated space. A logged overnight temperature excursion occurs; the pharmacist records the temperature but immediately returns all drug stock to saleable inventory, does not assess integrity, and plans to destroy temperature logs after 30 days. A staff member also stores lunch inside the unit. Which required changes are supported by 247 CMR 9.22? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Replace the prohibited dorm-style unit with qualifying equipment and follow Board temperature measurement guidance.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.22(2) prohibits a refrigerator with a freezer compartment within the refrigerator space, such as a dorm-style refrigerator.

choices.text: Release every affected product automatically because its printed expiration date has not passed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.22(1) requires a response protocol that assesses medication integrity after out-of-range temperature.

choices.text: Document the temperature excursion and product-integrity assessment and maintain required temperature log records for at least one year.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 9.22(1),(4) require excursion response/action documentation and minimum one-year records.

choices.text: Allow staff food and beverage in the medication refrigerator if placed on a separate shelf.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.22(5) prohibits any food or beverage in the medication refrigerator/freezer.

choices.text: Remove food and beverage from medication storage, and keep potentially affected drugs on hold until their integrity is appropriately assessed.
choices.why: Correct. This combines sections 9.22(1),(4),(5): integrity assessment and separation of food from medical stock.

questions.topic: Automated pharmacy vial-filling scanner malfunction: no verified automation output
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy uses Pharmacy Processing Automation (PPA) to count and label outpatient prescription vials. Its product barcode verification module has failed, and its backup automated weight and other technological verification sy
questions.legal_decision: Stop unverified PPA and use alternative properly validated manual process.
questions.critical_exception: All PPA technological verification safeguards have failed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a functioning approved technological verification remained operational and all other PPA requirements were met, continued PPA use could be considered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy uses Pharmacy Processing Automation (PPA) to count and label outpatient prescription vials. Its product barcode verification module has failed, and its backup automated weight and other technological verification systems are also unavailable. A technician proposes continuing to release vials through the PPA on the assumption that the machine is usually accurate. An on-duty pharmacist is available to use conventional manual dispensing workflows instead. What is the lawful response?

choices.text: Keep automated release unchanged because yesterday's quality assurance validation covers all future machine output.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prior QA record does not establish contemporaneous verification when all technological safeguards are unavailable.

choices.text: Let a certified technician override the final dispensing process validation whenever the automation audit log is blank.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technician certification does not confer pharmacist final validation authority.

choices.text: Record a fabricated machine barcode match for each package so that electronic output looks compliant.
choices.why: Incorrect. False system records cannot satisfy §9.11(1)(a) technological verification.

choices.text: Stop the unverified PPA dispensing workflow until required technological verification works; use a separate lawful manually validated process if needed.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.11(1)(a) conditions PPA use on technological verification for correct medication; section 9.04(1) still requires pharmacist final validation.

choices.text: Continue PPA because no federal law limits automated dispensing of Schedule VI medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts PPA requirements apply regardless of federal scheduling.

questions.topic: After-hours APS releases Schedule VI drug but lacks pharmacist consultation opportunity
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy operates an Automated Pharmacy System (APS) after its regular counter closes. The APS is secured, monitored and has a reliable patient-identification audit trail; it contains only room-temperature Schedule VI
questions.legal_decision: Stop after-hours APS dispensing during pharmacist-consultation outage.
questions.critical_exception: Machine product and physical safeguards are compliant; only counseling access fails.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an appropriate pharmacist consultation opportunity were restored during APS hours, that specific prohibition would no longer apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy operates an Automated Pharmacy System (APS) after its regular counter closes. The APS is secured, monitored and has a reliable patient-identification audit trail; it contains only room-temperature Schedule VI products. Tonight the contracted live pharmacist consultation service is offline and the pharmacy cannot provide any alternative real-time pharmacist consultation opportunity while the machine remains dispensing. Which conclusions are supported by 247 CMR 9.10? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Continue releasing prescriptions as usual because an audit trail is the only requirement after closing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.10(1)(g) separately requires a pharmacist consultation opportunity at every time the APS dispenses.

choices.text: Suspend APS dispensing until a pharmacist consultation opportunity is available during operation.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacy may not use APS for dispensing without the required consultation opportunity.

choices.text: Restoring accessible pharmacist consultation would correct this particular APS deficiency if all other conditions remain satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.10(1)(g) is the missing operation requirement in the scenario.

choices.text: A technician's prerecorded counseling voicemail is automatically equivalent to the required pharmacist consultation opportunity.
choices.why: Incorrect. An automated prerecorded technician message cannot itself substitute for access to a pharmacist.

choices.text: Dispense from APS only if the patient signs a waiver of every right to speak with a pharmacist.
choices.why: Incorrect. The section does not offer a patient waiver that eliminates the pharmacy's duty to provide a consultation opportunity.

questions.topic: Quarantined Schedule III product pending reverse distribution remains secured stock
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy has expired Schedule III medication awaiting reverse-distributor pickup. Staff move the quarantined bottles to an unlocked shelf in a general retail backroom, outside the secured prescription area, arguing that expi
questions.legal_decision: Maintain same controlled security for expired stock pending reverse distribution.
questions.critical_exception: Expiration and quarantine do not remove the controlled scheduling or storage rules.
questions.counterfactual_flip: After authorized transfer to a registered reverse distributor with proper records, on-site custody/security duties for the transferred units cease.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has expired Schedule III medication awaiting reverse-distributor pickup. Staff move the quarantined bottles to an unlocked shelf in a general retail backroom, outside the secured prescription area, arguing that expired drugs no longer count as controlled inventory. Which action complies with 247 CMR 9.21?

choices.text: Bring the expired drugs back into the secured prescription area and maintain controlled-substance security and disposition records until lawful transfer.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.21(1)–(2),(9)–(10) applies security/accountability duties to expired or quarantined drugs and those awaiting reverse distribution.

choices.text: Leave the bottles on the unlocked shelf if a 'not for dispensing' sign is posted.
choices.why: Incorrect. A label does not override the secured prescription area and controlled storage requirements.

choices.text: Discard the expired Schedule III drugs with ordinary pharmacy trash because no active patient prescription remains.
choices.why: Incorrect. Controlled-drug disposal requires approved registrant procedures and accurate records.

choices.text: Convert the medications into Schedule VI stock in the inventory system since they have expired.
choices.why: Incorrect. A drug's controlled schedule does not change because the expiration date passed.

choices.text: Ask a courier to take the stock directly to an unregistered private storage unit before reverse distribution.
choices.why: Incorrect. Unsecured off-site custody by an unauthorized party is not an authorized controlled disposal method.

questions.topic: Confirmed dispensing error creates shortage but not Board theft/loss report
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts resident pharmacy dispenses 30 Schedule IV tablets to the wrong patient, immediately confirms the DISPENSING ERROR in its records, and investigates; there is no evidence of theft, employee pilferage, or intentional diversion
questions.legal_decision: Document and remedy confirmed dispensing error through CQI rather than treating it as automatic theft.
questions.critical_exception: Confirmed accidental dispensing error; no theft/diversion or independently reportable serious injury.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If investigation instead confirms employee pilferage/theft, the RLCS and applicable DEA theft/loss duties arise under their separate rules.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts resident pharmacy dispenses 30 Schedule IV tablets to the wrong patient, immediately confirms the DISPENSING ERROR in its records, and investigates; there is no evidence of theft, employee pilferage, or intentional diversion, and no serious injury or other reporting trigger is present. The inventory now shows 30 fewer tablets than intended. A manager proposes automatically filing DEA Form 106 and a Board Pharmacy Loss Report for any such discrepancy without investigating the cause. What steps correctly distinguish the duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The dispensing error is automatically treated as a confirmed theft solely because the perpetual balance fell.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2026-01 §III distinguishes confirmed dispensing errors from theft/diversion; a quantity difference does not by itself establish theft.

choices.text: Document, investigate and address the dispensing error under the pharmacy's Continuous Quality Improvement process.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-01 §III expressly requires compliance with 247 CMR 15 CQI for confirmed dispensing errors.

choices.text: Report all confirmed dispensing errors as controlled-substance theft no matter the cause, without distinguishing theft from patient-safety error.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy says confirmed dispensing errors do not have to be reported under the loss/theft policy, though other separate harm-based duties may apply.

choices.text: Do not automatically submit the Board RLCS or federal theft/loss Form 106 solely for this confirmed non-theft dispensing error; investigate other separate reporting triggers.
choices.why: Correct. A confirmed dispensing error is excluded from the 2026-01 theft/loss reporting pathway; other duties remain independently applicable.

choices.text: Delete the patient profile to eliminate evidence of the incorrect dispensing transaction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Record destruction violates documentation and patient-safety duties and undermines quality improvement.

questions.citation: Board Policy 2026-01 §III; 247 CMR 15.00; 247 CMR 20.02 where serious injury applies
